newsitem.title: FRANCE: Attacks mount on Renault, workers protest job cuts.
newsitem.headline: Attacks mount on Renault, workers protest job cuts.

text.p: Workers disrupted production at the largest Renault plant on Thursday to protest against the carmaker's plans to cut jobs amid mounting calls for chairman Louis Schweitzer's resignation.
Political leaders kept hammering at Schweitzer's handling of the announcement of the closure of a Belgian plant employing 3,100 people and 2,764 job cuts in France this year.
President Jacques Chirac, on a trip to Brazil, repeated his criticism that the closure announcement was poorly handled but said plant shutdowns were "an unfortunate fact of life."
Other officials in France called for Schweitzer's resignation.

Belgian Prime Minister Dehaene reiterated his government's condemnation of the plant closure in the Brussels suburbs. The Belga news agency quoted him as saying in a letter to Schweitzer that Belgium "does not accept either the closure of the Vilvoorde plant or the procedure used to announce the decision."
Schweitzer says Renault respected Belgian and European laws in announcing the closure and gave as much warning as required.
A Renault spokeswoman declined to comment on the calls for his resignation, which she called a "political debate."

Unions also stepped up pressure on the management. Renault's French staff committee voted to delay a study of the job-cutting plan, which had been on the agenda for Thursday, until April 3 after the committee secretary requested expert counsel.

Unions had called on Renault workers to stage labour stoppages on Thursday, but Renault said the call was observed at only one of Renault's 17 French sites. Workers in Flins, which produces the Clio and Twingo cars, struck for one and a half hours. "There was very little disruption," the spokeswoman said.

An official at the CGT union, the biggest at Renault, said disruption was more widespread. He said workers staged stoppages in the Grand Couronne components plant in Normandy and the Lardy test centre. Production was briefly interrupted at Douai, which makes the new Megane cars, when 300 workers from Belgium staged a solidarity demonstration with French workers.
Unions are planning industry-wide labour action that would also target PSA Peugeot Citroen and equipment suppliers on March 20, the day Renault is due to announce heavy losses for 1996.
A senior politician in France's ruling coalition said that Schweitzer had committed an "irreparable mistake" in the way he announced the Vilvoorde plant closure and should quit.

Jean-Francois Mancel, secretary-general and number two to Prime Minister Alain Juppe in the conservative Gaullist party, told Europe 1 radio that Schweitzer had "committed a very serious mistake by offending human dignity."

"Whatever necessities an employer may face in having to make people redundant, he must not fail to respect the employees as human beings. Coming from a very big captain of industry, this is an irreparable mistake and he should take the consequences," Mancel said.

Mancel, who often reflects Juppe's views, was the most senior politician to call for the resignation of Schweitzer, a former top civil servant who moved to Renault after serving as top aide to Socialist prime minister Laurent Fabius in 1984-86.
Schweitzer also came under fire from the author of a law that gives incentives to companies that reduce work hours to preserve jobs in France, which has 12.7 percent unemployment.
Responding to a comment by Schweitzer that the law was only suitable for temporary situations, lawmaker Gilles de Robien said: "Chairmen, too, are temporary."
The Renault board confirmed Schweitzer's mandate last July at its first meeting after the French state gave up majority control. He had been re-appointed in May 1994 for five years.
The state is still the biggest shareholder with 46 percent but Juppe has insisted that the management is free to take business decisions without government intervention.
